content: Maid in Mistress Ansell's house in Great St Helen's
She wants a speech, and she is the one who thinks of the washing.
She cannot letter a parcel, and she does not pretend she can.
She can see a short loaf without being able to read the bill, and she will say the shortfall to her mistress before she says it to you.
She has never seen a play, and she finds the hole in an oath by asking who cooks.
Warwickshire is a hundred miles, and she has never been ten. She can hold that pair of numbers without asking to read the page.
She had one band starched blue, from Whitsun last, and she washed it white when she was allowed.
She wants the edge of a rule named, and she will ask for it at the church door when no one else does.
She can keep the churchyard she saw apart from the shops and Ludgate she only heard.
Cutting the loaf four ways, she said cutting does not make it larger.
She said the glass told the truth, and that he should have kept it.
She prices a line the way a crier prices a flower, and she knows the girl at the window and the boy who plays her are differently hurt.
She asks which sorrow the line is, and then she tells you how to say the end, and then she is called off the stair.
She can start a riddle and stop before the answer, and she measures the penny loaf against the notch without being asked.
She cuts a length on her own arm, and she measures the penny loaf against the notch without being asked.
Alse can hold a question from one afternoon to the next morning. She now knows the one who dies is a boy of fifteen, lodged in Aldermanbury, who ate two pies. She treats that as the wonderful part.
